structure.title: I
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Jay Gatsby, Nick Carraway, reflecting on his father’s advice to reserve judgment due to unequal advantages in life, which shaped his tendency to become a confidant for others’ intimate revelations and later led to his disillusionment with the moral chaos of privileged society after returning from the East last autumn—except for Gatsby, whom he admires for his extraordinary gift for hope and romantic readiness. In the spring of 1922, Nick moves alone to West Egg to learn the bond business, renting a modest eighty-dollar bungalow between two lavish estates; he feels isolated until a stranger asks him for directions to West Egg village, granting him a sense of belonging. That evening, he drives by car to East Egg to dine with his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom, a physically imposing Yale acquaintance, at their opulent Georgian Colonial home, where he meets the enigmatic Jordan Baker reclining on a couch with Daisy, whose melodic voice masks restless energy. During dinner, Tom introduces racist pseudoscience from The Rise of the Coloured Empires, Daisy fabricates a story about the butler’s nose after a telephone call, and Jordan reveals in confidence that Tom has a mistress in New York; Daisy later confesses her cynical belief that a woman’s best fate is to be a 'beautiful little fool,' while Nick observes the strained dynamics as Tom and Jordan retreat to the library. As Nick departs, Daisy teases him about marrying Jordan, Tom criticizes her independence, and they press him about unfounded rumors of his engagement to a girl out West—denied by Nick, who drives home to West Egg and sits on an abandoned grass roller, only to see Gatsby standing alone on his lawn, arms outstretched toward a single green light across the bay, trembling before vanishing into the darkness.

structure.title: II
structure.summary: On a summer Sunday afternoon, Nick Carraway travels by train with Tom Buchanan to the valley of ashes, where Tom forcibly introduces him to Myrtle Wilson at her husband George B. Wilson’s run-down garage; they then journey separately to New York, with Myrtle riding alone to avoid scrutiny, purchasing magazines, perfume, and impulsively buying a dog from a street vendor—insisting it is male despite Tom’s correction—before boarding a lavender taxicab. The group arrives at Myrtle’s overcrowded rented apartment on 158th Street, where she calls her sister Catherine and Mr. McKee, serves whisky, and transforms into a cream chiffon dress, adopting an artificial air of hauteur as guests arrive: Catherine with plucked eyebrows and jangling bracelets, and the McKees, whose wife is loud and vain while Mr. McKee is shy and later analyzes Myrtle’s features for a portrait under the blurred gaze of her mother’s photograph. As the party descends into drunken chaos, Myrtle defiantly repeats Daisy’s name, provoking Tom to violently break her nose, sparking panic as women scramble for towels and Myrtle bleeds while covering her face with Town Tattle magazine; Mr. McKee awakens dazed, invites Nick to lunch, and Nick ultimately escapes into the cold, dim interior of Pennsylvania Station, exhausted and disoriented, waiting for the four o’clock train after witnessing the brutal collapse of Myrtle’s fantasy of escape.

structure.title: III
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway arriving by car at Jay Gatsby’s Long Island mansion on a Saturday evening shortly after seven, where he is immersed in a chaotic, opulent party fueled by champagne, live orchestra performances, and weekly deliveries of five crates of fruit discarded as pulp. Amid rumors that Gatsby killed a man or was a German spy, Nick Carraway encounters a drunken guest in the library who marvels at the authenticity of Gatsby’s unread books with uncut pages, and later bonds with a fellow war veteran who owns a hydroplane—yet still has not met Gatsby. After being introduced to Jordan Baker, Nick Carraway learns the man he has been speaking with is Gatsby himself, who politely invites him to fly in the hydroplane the next morning before being called away by a phone call from Chicago; as the party descends into chaos—with a woman singing while weeping ink-tears, marriages unraveling, and a new coupe crashing into a wall with a dazed passenger emerging unaware of the damage—Nick Carraway departs to find Gatsby standing alone on the porch, formally bidding farewell under a faint moon. In a reflective interlude, Nick Carraway recounts his daily routine in New York: working at the Probity Trust, dining with clerks in dark restaurants, studying investments at the Yale Club while avoiding rowdy guests, and walking home past Madison Avenue to Pennsylvania Station, where he romanticizes strangers on Fifth Avenue but feels profound loneliness; his reconnection with Jordan Baker turns disillusioning after he learns of her dishonesty—lying about damaging a borrowed car and recalling her scandal of moving a golf ball in a tournament—while he continues writing weekly letters signed 'Love, Nick' to a woman back home, remembering the perspiration on her upper lip during tennis, ultimately declaring himself one of the few honest people he has known.

structure.title: IV
structure.summary: On a Sunday morning in July 1922, Gatsby’s mansion hosts a chaotic, glittering party attended by a vast array of guests from East Egg, West Egg, and New York, arriving by car, including the Chester Beckers, Klipspringer, Benny McClenahan with four identical girls, and Henry L. Palmetto, whose suicide is noted as a detached footnote; rumors circulate wildly, including that Gatsby killed a man connected to Von Hindenburg and the devil. Later that same month, Gatsby arrives at Nick Carraway’s door in his cream-colored car with a three-noted horn, invites him to lunch, and during the drive through Queens past the valley of ashes and Blackwell’s Island, reveals an elaborate, implausible backstory—claiming Oxford education, European aristocratic travels, wartime heroism in the Argonne Forest, and a Montenegrin Orderi di Danilo medal, which he produces as proof, before requesting Nick Carraway arrange a meeting with Jordan Baker. At noon in a cellar restaurant on Forty-second Street, Gatsby introduces Nick Carraway to Meyer Wolfshiem, a grotesque figure with hair growing from his nostrils and cuff buttons made of human molars, who recounts in vivid detail the murder of Rosy Rosenthal at the old Metropole; Gatsby deflects Wolfshiem’s attempt to involve Nick Carraway in business, then abruptly leaves to make a phone call, reappearing briefly after a tense encounter with Tom Buchanan, who is unaware of Gatsby’s identity. In a flashback to October 1917, Jordan Baker recalls encountering Daisy Fay in her white roadster with Lieutenant Jay Gatsby in Louisville, where Daisy was deeply enamored; years later, after Daisy’s lavish marriage to Tom Buchanan—marked by a $350,000 string of pearls she nearly rejected while drunk the night before—and Tom’s subsequent infidelities, Jordan learns in 1923 that the name Gatsby refers to the same officer from 1917. After leaving the Plaza Hotel at twilight, Jordan reveals to Nick Carraway that Gatsby bought his mansion solely so Daisy could see the green light across the bay, and he now wants Nick Carraway to invite Daisy to tea so he can visit her unknowingly, having feared offending Nick Carraway upon learning of his connection to Tom; as they drive through Central Park in a victoria, Nick Carraway becomes distracted by Jordan’s presence, tightening his hold on her as they pass Fifty-Ninth Street, internally repeating, 'There are only the pursued, the pursuing, the busy, and the tired.'

structure.title: V
structure.summary: The chapter begins with Nick returning to his West Egg home at night to find Gatsby’s mansion brilliantly lit but silent, where Gatsby nervously invites him to Coney Island or a swim before asking him to arrange a tea meeting with Daisy; the next day, rain falls as Gatsby sends a man to cut Nick’s lawn and arrives in a white flannel suit, visibly anxious, awaiting Daisy’s arrival by car with her chauffeur Ferdie; upon her arrival, Gatsby is so overwhelmed he nearly knocks over a clock, but after an excruciatingly awkward reunion, Nick leaves briefly and returns to find Daisy crying and Gatsby radiating quiet joy, leading him to enthusiastically invite her to tour his mansion, where they walk down to the road and enter through the big postern, admiring its feudal architecture, gardens, and floral scents; inside, they pass silent, opulent rooms—including Marie Antoinette music-rooms and Restoration Salons—until they encounter Mr. Klipspringer in pajamas doing exercises; Gatsby then displays his collection of luxurious shirts, which overwhelms Daisy into tears, causing Gatsby to watch her with dazed awe as his dream becomes real; later, as rain resumes, Gatsby points out the green light at Daisy’s dock, now diminished in symbolic power, shows Nick a photograph of Mr. Dan Cody and a youthful picture of himself in yachting attire, and shares newspaper clippings about Daisy, which they examine together; Klipspringer is summoned to play piano, nervously performing 'The Love Nest' and 'One Thing’s Sure' as thunder rolls and West Egg lights up with electric trains returning from New York, during which Nick observes Gatsby’s growing realization that Daisy cannot fulfill his idealized vision, yet he remains captivated by her voice until Nick departs alone into the rain, leaving them lost in each other.

structure.title: VI
structure.summary: A New York reporter arrives at Gatsby’s mansion seeking a statement, drawn by escalating rumors—including that Gatsby lives in a boat disguised as a house—revealing his growing notoriety; the narrative then shifts to Gatsby’s origins as James Gatz of North Dakota, who, at seventeen, rowed out to Dan Cody’s yacht Tuolomee on Lake Superior in a torn green jersey and canvas pants, spent five years serving Cody in multiple roles aboard the boat, learned to avoid alcohol after witnessing its destructive effects, and emerged with a new identity after being disinherited by Ella Kaye following Cody’s death. Weeks later, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s mansion on a Sunday afternoon when Tom Buchanan, Mr. Sloane, and a woman in a brown riding-habit arrive on horseback; Gatsby nervously offers drinks and tries to connect with Tom by mentioning their prior meeting and asserting he knows Daisy, but Tom and Sloane respond with cold condescension, and when the woman invites them to supper, Sloane subtly blocks Gatsby’s participation before they depart abruptly. The following Saturday night, Tom and Daisy attend Gatsby’s party, where Tom’s presence creates an oppressive atmosphere: Daisy is both fascinated and appalled by West Egg’s excess, while Tom dismisses guests as bootleggers; after dancing, Gatsby and Daisy sit alone on Nick Carraway’s steps, and Gatsby reveals his desperate belief that he can repeat the past by having Daisy declare she never loved Tom, a hope rooted in his idealized memory of their first kiss under moonlight five years earlier.

structure.title: VII
structure.summary: On the hottest day of summer, Nick arrives by train at the Buchanans’ estate to find Gatsby waiting, having dismissed all original servants and replaced them with Meyer Wolfsheim’s relatives to conceal Daisy’s secret visits. During lunch, Daisy openly kisses Gatsby while Tom watches in stunned silence; later, the group departs in separate cars—Tom insists Gatsby drive his own vehicle, revealing distrust, as Tom reveals he has investigated Gatsby’s past and dismissed his Oxford claims. The group travels to Wilson’s garage in the valley of ashes under oppressive heat, where a sick and emotionally broken George Wilson, unaware of his wife Myrtle’s affair, asks about buying Tom’s car while Myrtle watches from the window, mistaking Jordan for Tom’s wife. The tension erupts further at the Plaza Hotel in New York, where Tom accuses Gatsby of bootlegging through Wolfsheim’s drugstores, and Daisy, overwhelmed, admits she once loved Tom but also loved Gatsby before retreating into silence; Tom orders them to return to Long Island together in Gatsby’s car. Later, Myrtle rushes out of the garage and is struck by a speeding yellow car that flees, killing her instantly with horrific trauma; Michaelis witnesses the event and reports the car as light green to police. Tom and Nick arrive at the scene to find Wilson distraught, crying 'Oh, my Ga-od!' as witnesses describe the yellow car; Tom, relieved his blue coupé is not implicated, quietly urges Nick to leave, then breaks down in tears calling the driver a coward. Finally, Nick waits outside the Buchanans’ house alone, where Gatsby emerges in his pink suit, confessing Daisy was driving the fatal car and he intends to take the blame; Nick sees Tom and Daisy inside the kitchen sharing food in quiet intimacy, while Gatsby remains outside, vigilantly watching, unaware that Daisy has chosen Tom and his dream is over.

structure.title: VIII
structure.summary: At dawn on Long Island, Nick Carraway, unable to sleep due to the foghorn, finds Gatsby dejected in his mansion’s hallway after waiting all night for Daisy to appear at her window—she briefly looked out, then turned off the light. Inside the vast, dusty house, they search for cigarettes and smoke by open French windows as Nick Carraway urges Gatsby to flee to Atlantic City or Montreal to avoid being traced, but Gatsby refuses, clinging to the hope that Daisy will choose him. Gatsby recounts his youth with Dan Cody and his first meeting with Daisy, admitting he misled her about his wealth and social status, binding himself irrevocably to a dream she left behind. On the last afternoon before his departure abroad, Gatsby and Daisy shared a silent, profound embrace in a firelit room, their connection so deep no words were needed. After the war, Gatsby was mistakenly sent to Oxford while Daisy, overwhelmed by her opulent social world of orchids and all-night parties, grew desperate and chose Tom Buchanan, whose solid presence offered her the decisive force she craved; the letter informing Gatsby of her decision reached him at Oxford. Later, Gatsby insists Daisy never truly loved Tom, attributing her reaction to fear, and recalls his painful journey by day-coach to Louisville after their wedding, walking the streets where he had known her, feeling he had left her behind. At nine a.m., he reveals he never used his pool all summer; Nick Carraway, missing two trains, finally departs, shouting that Gatsby is worth more than 'the whole damn bunch put together,' receiving a radiant smile in return. Meanwhile, Wilson, consumed by grief after Myrtle’s death, fixates on the yellow car and the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg, declaring 'God sees everything.' He walks to Port Roosevelt and Gad’s Hill, buys food, vanishes for three hours—possibly searching garages for the car—and arrives in West Egg asking for Gatsby’s house. At two p.m., Gatsby dons his bathing suit, retrieves a pneumatic mattress from the garage with the chauffeur’s help, instructs the butler to bring any call to him at the pool, and orders the damaged car left untouched. He carries the mattress alone toward the pool as the butler waits in vain for a call that never comes. The chauffeur hears gunshots but dismisses them; Nick Carraway rushes from the station and alerts others. Four men—chauffeur, butler, gardener, and narrator—find Gatsby’s body floating on the mattress in the pool, and the gardener discovers Wilson’s body in the grass, completing the holocaust.

structure.title: IX
structure.summary: After Gatsby’s death, police, photographers, and reporters swarm his mansion, where sensationalized newspaper reports frame Wilson as a 'madman' and Catherine denies any connection between Myrtle and Gatsby, simplifying the tragedy. Nick Carraway, isolated and burdened by guilt, desperately tries to reach Daisy and Meyer Wolfsheim—receiving no response from either, even after a mistaken long-distance call assumes Gatsby is alive. On the third day, Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives by train from Minnesota, visibly frail and in shock; he is shown Gatsby’s mansion and reads aloud from Gatsby’s childhood self-improvement schedule in a worn copy of Hopalong Cassidy, expressing quiet pride. Klipspringer calls to request his tennis shoes and declines to attend the funeral, while Wolfsheim refuses to come, claiming he avoids being 'mixed up' in deaths. At the funeral, only Gatz, the minister, four or five servants, and the West Egg postman are present; as rain falls, the man with owl-eyed glasses—whom Nick Carraway met months earlier in Gatsby’s library—appears unexpectedly, wiping rain from his glasses to view the grave and murmuring 'Amen to that' after hearing 'Blessed are the dead that the rain falls on,' then lamenting that no one else came. Later, Nick Carraway encounters Tom Buchanan on Fifth Avenue, who admits he told Wilson Gatsby owned the car that killed Myrtle, justifying it as retribution; Tom’s performative grief over dog biscuits reveals his moral emptiness, which Nick Carraway recognizes as part of a pattern with Tom and Daisy as 'careless people.' After selling his car and packing, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s empty house at night, erasing an obscene word scrawled on the steps, then walks to the beach where he reflects on Gatsby’s pursuit of the green light and concludes with the metaphor of boats beaten back ceaselessly into the past.

plot_summary.plot_summary:
Jay Gatsby, reflecting from the vantage of time, recounts his journey from James Gatz of North Dakota to the enigmatic millionaire of West Egg, driven by an unwavering dream to reclaim a lost love. In the spring of 1922, he buys a grand mansion across the bay from Daisy Buchanan—his former flame from Louisville in 1917—so that he might one day see the green light at the end of her dock. Through Nick Carraway, his neighbor and reluctant confidant, Gatsby orchestrates a reunion with Daisy, rekindling their romance beneath the opulence of his parties and the illusion of his fabricated aristocratic past. Yet beneath the glittering surface, Gatsby’s identity is built on myth: his Oxford education, war medals, and wealth are all carefully curated to match the world Daisy inhabits, even as he clings to the belief that the past can be repeated and love restored exactly as it was.

As Gatsby’s dream intensifies, the world around him begins to fracture. Daisy, now married to the brutish Tom Buchanan, is pulled between her lingering affection for Gatsby and the security of her privileged life. Their affair becomes public during a scorching summer day at the Plaza Hotel, where Daisy’s confession that she once loved Tom—and her subsequent retreat into silence—shatters Gatsby’s illusion. The collision of their worlds leads to tragedy: Myrtle Wilson, Tom’s mistress, is killed by a speeding yellow car, though Daisy is behind the wheel. Gatsby, refusing to let go, takes the blame, believing Daisy will choose him in the aftermath. But as he waits for her call from his mansion, Daisy retreats into Tom’s embrace, leaving Gatsby exposed and alone. Meanwhile, George Wilson, Myrtle’s grieving husband, misled by Tom into believing Gatsby was both Myrtle’s lover and her killer, seeks vengeance.

In the quiet dawn after the storm, Gatsby stands watch outside Daisy’s house, still holding onto the hope that she will reach out—until his dream dissolves with the morning light. He is shot by Wilson at his pool, a victim not of crime but of the impossible ideal he spent his life pursuing. Though he survives to tell this story, the weight of his loss lingers in every word. Nick Carraway, the only one who truly understood him, organizes a funeral that no one attends except Gatsby’s father, a humble man who reads from his son’s childhood schedule with quiet pride. As Gatsby reflects on the emptiness of the East and the moral decay of its elite, he sees himself not as a fool, but as a man who dared to believe in something pure. He ends his tale by gazing at the bay, remembering how every boat is borne back ceaselessly into the past—not because it fails, but because hope, even when broken, is the only thing that moves us forward.
